texts.preamble: M/S. Ferrous Traders vs The Managing Director on 7 March, 2019 Author: Shaji P.Chaly Bench: Shaji P.Chaly In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present The Honourable Mr. Justice Shaji P.Chaly Thursday ,The 07Th Day Of March 2019 / 16Th Phalguna, 1940 WP(C).No. 25110 of 2013 Petitioner/S: M/S. Ferrous Traders, Represented By Its Proprietor, Shri. Faizal Abdul Samad, Aged 45 Years, S/O. Abdul Samad, Viii/292, Kottayil Kovilakam, Chendamangalam, Ernakulam District-683 502. By Advs. Sri.P.A.Augustian Sri.M.A.Baby Sri.V.K.Sathyanathan Respondent/S: 1 The Managing Director, Cargo Freight Station, Petta- 682038. 2 Commissioner Of Customs, Customs House, W/Island, Cochin-9. 3 Addl. Commissioner Of Customs (Preventive), Rummage & Intelligence Division, Willington Island, Cochin-682 003. *Addl.
texts.facts: To issue a writ of mandamus directing the respondent No.2 to initiate appropriate proceedings against respondent No.1 since they failed to comply with Ext.P6 Regulation by exempting petitioner from payment of detention/demurrage charge for goods seized/confiscated by respondent No.2 and 3; and III. Grant such other reliefs that this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case." 2. Brief material facts for the disposal of the writ petition are as follows: 3. Petitioner is a trader involved in import of materials through Cochin Port. During the course of trade, petitioner imported Potato Powder (Starch) from abroad through Cochin Port and filed Bills M/S. Ferrous Traders vs The Managing Director on 7 March, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/111193800/ 2 of Entry for its clearance. The value of the potato powder was Rs.5,96,797/-. The Customs authority confirmed the value and assessed customs duty at Rs.2,84,140/-. According to the petitioner, due to his inability to pay customs duty as assessed by the Customs authority, petitioner requested for removal and storage of the goods to respondent No.1. When the petitioner managed sufficient fund to clear the goods, 3rd respondent, i.e., the Additional Commissioner of Customs made allegations regarding the quality of the goods. It is also alleged that the petitioner is indulging in illegal import of such goods for unlawful gain. Though the petitioner made detailed submissions and expressed willingness to conduct examination of the goods through any authorised agency, 3rd respondent did not allow such request and proceeded with investigation. 4. It is also the case of the petitioner that, the Director, Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore found that the samples confirmed to the standards laid down for food articles under Sea Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and Rule 2011 thereon. Since there was no such illegality as alleged, the adjudication authority allowed to release the goods as per Ext.P1 order. However, to cover up the unlawful detention of the goods over a considerable period, fresh allegation regarding mis-declaration of 191 packages of potato powder was made and the goods were ordered to be confiscated and allowed to redeem the same on applicable customs duty with interest thereon. In addition to that, penalty of Rs.15,000/- was also imposed under Sec.112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. 5. Accordingly, petitioner paid the penalty and sought release of the goods. However, due to detention of goods, 1st respondent is demanding huge amounts towards demurrage charges. The point put forth by the petitioner is that, as per Sec.6(1) of Ext.P6 Regulations, the 1st respondent being a Customs Cargo Service provider have no right to charge any rent or demurrage on the goods seized or detained or confiscated by proper officer under respondent Nos.2 and 3, and any such demand shall amount to violating the aforesaid regulation attracting penal action. Petitioner has also sought for waiver before respondent No.2 and to issue a certificate of waiver of demurrage charge. Even though petitioner has taken up the matter with the 3rd respondent, as per letter dated 25.07.2013, no action was initiated. However, 1st respondent as per Ext.P5 e-mail communication dated 13.09.2013 intimated that they are willing to extend 20% rebate on the total ground rent charges subject to the condition that the entire items should be released from the godown on or before 10.10.2013. Therefore, now the case put forth by the petitioner is that, the goods shall be released to the petitioner without insisting for any demurrage charges. 6. Statements are filed by the 1st respondent, justifying the stand adopted by them insisting the petitioner to pay the demurrage charges. According to the 1st respondent, an amount of Rs.15,29,795/- is due from the petitioner. It is also pointed out that, petitioner is liable to pay demurrage charges, even though petitioner has a contention that regulation 6(1) (1) of Ext.P6 Regulations attracts, to the benefit of the petitioner. That apart, it is submitted that, petitioner was informed by the 1st respondent as per Annexure-C notice to pay the demurrage charges on ground rent and clear the goods as early as on 10.11.2010. Since the petitioner has not responded to the same, 1st respondent has issued Annexure-D letter, requesting the petitioner to clear the goods after paying the demurrage charges. However, petitioner as per Annexure-E letter sought time and requested not to auction the goods. Respondents 2 and 3 have also filed a detailed counter affidavit almost in similar lines with that of the 1st respondent, and also stating that petitioner is liable to pay demurrage charges in order to release the goods.
texts.arguments: 9. The paramount contention advanced by the petitioner is relying upon Regulation (6) of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009, wherein the responsibilities of Customs Cargo Service provider are delineated. Clause (l) thereunder is relevant to the context, which read thus: "(l) subject to any other law for the time being in force, shall not charge any rent or demurrage on the goods seized or detained or confiscated by the proper officer." Therefore, relying upon the said provision, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that, the Customs authorities are not entitled under law to compel the petitioner to pay the demurrage charges. However, learned counsel appearing for the respondents submitted that, here is a case where the Customs authorities have seized the goods and directed the 1st respondent to keep the goods in safe custody. I find force in the contention advanced by learned counsel for the respondents, since the 1st respondent is an independent body carrying on with the business of storing goods for and on behalf of customers. Therefore, when goods are entrusted to the 1st respondent, 1st respondent is entitled as of right to seek demurrage charges.
texts.petitioner_arguments: 9. The paramount contention advanced by the petitioner is relying upon Regulation (6) of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009, wherein the responsibilities of Customs Cargo Service provider are delineated. Clause (l) thereunder is relevant to the context, which read thus: "(l) subject to any other law for the time being in force, shall not charge any rent or demurrage on the goods seized or detained or confiscated by the proper officer."
texts.respondent_arguments: Therefore, relying upon the said provision, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that, the Customs authorities are not entitled under law to compel the petitioner to pay the demurrage charges. However, learned counsel appearing for the respondents submitted that, here is a case where the Customs authorities have seized the goods and directed the 1st respondent to keep the goods in safe custody. I find force in the contention advanced by learned counsel for the respondents, since the 1st respondent is an independent body carrying on with the business of storing goods for and on behalf of customers. Therefore, when goods are entrusted to the 1st respondent, 1st respondent is entitled as of right to seek demurrage charges.
